The ROC curve trades sensitivity against (1 − specificity) across every score threshold, summarized by AUC; the precision–recall curve shows the same ranking from the positive-class perspective and is the honest display under class imbalance. Julia's MLJ has MLJBase receivers for metrics, but the curves themselves are a threshold sweep — fifteen lines of base Julia plus `CairoMakie`.

## Example

![](../images/Julia/RocPrPlot_demo.png){fig-align="center" width="80%"}

## Setup

- System Requirements: Cross-platform (Linux/MacOS/Windows)
- Programming Language: **Julia**
- Dependencies: `CairoMakie`, `DataFrames`, `Statistics`

```{julia}
#| label: packages-setup
#| output: false
using CairoMakie
using DataFrames
using Statistics
using Random
```

## Data Preparation

We simulate diagnostic scores for 2,000 patients with 10% prevalence: healthy scores centred at 0, diseased scores shifted upward.

```{julia}
#| label: data-prep
Random.seed!(161)

n = 2000; prevalence = 0.10
label = rand(n) .< prevalence
scores = ifelse.(label, 0.9 .+ 0.55 .* randn(n), 0.65 .* randn(n))

function roc_pr_curve(label, scores)
    order = sortperm(scores; rev = true)
    y = label[order]
    tp = cumsum(y); fp = cumsum(.!y)
    P = sum(y); N = length(y) - P
    tpr = tp ./ P
    fpr = fp ./ N
    recall = tpr
    precision = tp ./ (tp .+ fp)
    auc = sum(diff(fpr) .* (tpr[1:end-1] .+ tpr[2:end]) ./ 2)
    ap = sum(precision[i] * (recall[i-1] - recall[i]) for i in 2:length(recall))
    (tpr, fpr, auc, precision, recall, ap)
end
tpr, fpr, auc_value, precision, recall, ap = roc_pr_curve(label, scores)
```

## Visualization

### ROC Curve with AUC

The AUC here uses the trapezoid rule over the swept (FPR, TPR) path; the diagonal is the chance classifier.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-jl-roc
#| fig-cap: "ROC curve with the chance diagonal and trapezoid AUC"
#| width: 460
fig = Figure(size = (450, 430))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "False positive rate",
          ylabel = "True positive rate")
lines!(ax, fpr, tpr; color = :tomato, linewidth = 1.9,
       label = "AUC = $(round(auc_value; digits = 3))")
lines!(ax, [0, 1], [0, 1]; color = :gray50, linewidth = 0.9,
       linestyle = :dash, label = "Chance")
axislegend(ax; framevisible = false, position = :rb)
ylims!(ax, 0, 1.02)
hidespines!(ax, :t, :r)
fig
```

### Precision–Recall Curve

With 10% prevalence the chance precision sits at 0.10 (dashed) — a strong ROC can look far less flattering here, which is the point.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-jl-pr
#| fig-cap: "Precision-recall curve with average precision and prevalence baseline"
#| width: 460
fig = Figure(size = (450, 430))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "Recall", ylabel = "Precision")
lines!(ax, recall, precision; color = :steelblue, linewidth = 1.9,
       label = "AP = $(round(ap; digits = 3))")
hlines!(ax, [prevalence]; color = :gray50, linewidth = 0.9,
        linestyle = :dash, label = "Prevalence = 0.10")
axislegend(ax; framevisible = false, position = :rt)
ylims!(ax, 0, 1.02)
hidespines!(ax, :t, :r)
fig
```

1. Fawcett, T. (2006). An introduction to ROC analysis. *Pattern Recognition Letters*, 27(8), 861-874.
2. Saito, T., & Rehmsmeier, M. (2015). The Precision-Recall Plot Is More Informative than the ROC Plot When Evaluating Binary Classifiers on Imbalanced Datasets. *PLoS ONE*, 10(3), e0118432.
